name: WAMR (WebAssembly Micro Runtime) fast interpreter
baseline: wasmtime Pulley interpreter
workload: Same 39-case interpreter harness as the wasm3 entry (17 cases common to all runtimes): CPU time per call on M4 Max and iPhone XS Max E-cores with JIT/AOT disabled.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to fastest: WAMR 1.63 vs Pulley 2.09 on M4 Max E-cores (about 1.28x faster, derived from page data) and 1.38 vs 1.68 on iPhone XS (about 1.22x, derived). Per case on M4: bulk_memory 10.41 vs 22.14 ms, call_indirect 18.48 vs 31.53 ms, convolution 3.928 vs 5.883 ms, sieve 0.5128 vs 0.7082 ms. Separately, the repo's own cross-runtime doc says WAMR is 1.37-1.86x faster than Pulley on iPhone 12 across call_indirect, xmrsplayer, vtable and graphql (AssemblyScript).
compiler_and_flags: cmake Release, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 etc., WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1, Apple clang 21.0.0; 29 local patches applied to WAMR main b70d708d (2026-09-21).
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (macOS 27.0) and iPhone XS Max (A12 Bionic)
tradeoffs: Fast-interpreter mode only in this comparison (AOT and JIT disabled by the App-Store constraint). Footprint about 58.9K for the fast interpreter per README. The measured build lacks GC, typed references, memory64, multi-memory and exnref.
caveats: The win is interpreter versus wasmtime's Pulley interpreter, not versus wasmtime's native Cranelift JIT, which is far faster than both. WAMR is also slower than wasm3 in the same harness (1.63 vs 1.01 geomean) and than wasm3 in the 2021 libsodium shootout, and the wasmz benchmark shows it behind wasmz and wasm3. The Pulley build carries the harness author's own optimization patches (9 commits), so Pulley is if anything flattered. WAMR itself is also a baseline named for this category, so treat as a relative claim.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (site filter github.com) surfaced rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark

name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter; wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: 39-case interpreter harness (17 cases that every runtime runs): fib, sieve, crc32, call_indirect, vtable dispatch, xmrsplayer tracker player, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP; CPU time per call at N=10 on E-cores of an M4 Max and an iPhone XS Max, JIT/AOT disabled in all runtimes.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geomean over 17 cases: wasm3 1.01, wamr 1.63, wasmtime Pulley 2.09, wasmz 1.59, tinywasm 3.20, WasmEdge 8.42 on M4 Max E-cores (about 1.6x faster than WAMR and 2.1x faster than Pulley, derived from page data); iPhone XS: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68. call_indirect: wasm3 11.67 ms vs WAMR 18.48 ms vs Pulley 31.53 ms per call (M4). The 2021 libsodium shootout also says WAMR 'was slower than wasm3 on every single test'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions on Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27); WAMR main b70d708d with cmake Release -O3 and AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off; Pulley from wasmtime v49 fork with --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO.
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (macOS 27.0) and iPhone XS Max (A12 Bionic) E-cores
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with a small footprint (about 64 KB code, 10 KB RAM per README); it cannot run SIMD, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, so it only ran 20-odd of the 39 harness cases. README says the repo is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3's own docs/Performance.md (2019-2020, i5-8250U, CoreMark) shows wasmtime 4.0x and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster than wasm3, and WAMR 8.1x slower, so JIT runtimes still win on sustained compute. In the 2026 harness wasm3's instantiate cost on extended-const modules is 116-122x Pulley's. The harness author maintains a wasmtime fork and applies 29 patches to WAMR and 26 to WasmEdge, but none to wasm3 (v0.9.0 unpatched). Compared to Pulley it is not wasmtime's native JIT.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (site filter github.com) surfaced rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark and wasm3 docs/Performance.md

name: zwasm
baseline: wasmtime 43.0.1; wasmer 5.0.4; wazero 1.11.0; WasmEdge 0.16.1 (interpreter)
workload: End-to-end wall time of '<runtime> run <module>' (spawn, instantiate, execute WASI _start) with hyperfine on short TinyGo and ClojureWasm guests, plus peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
claimed_speedup: Startup-bound short workloads (mean ms): tinygo/fib zwasm-aot 2.0, interp 2.3, jit 2.8 vs wasmtime 7.2, wazero 7.1, wasmer 12.0, WasmEdge 16.5. Peak RSS on tinygo/fib: zwasm-aot 2.1 MB, jit 3.2, interp 2.7 vs wazero 8.7, wasmtime 13.3, WasmEdge 23.7, wasmer 27.5 ('4-12x less').
compiler_and_flags: zwasm built ReleaseFast (Zig); comparators pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (Mac aarch64), one host
tradeoffs: Single-pass JIT, interpreter and AOT backends with Wasm 3.0 and WASI 0.2/0.3; small footprint and fast startup traded for peak throughput.
caveats: The doc is explicit that the optimizing JITs lead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; base64 about 13.7x slower). The startup rows are dominated by process start, not execution. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark found zwasm's interpreter about 8.5x slower than the fastest interpreter (geomean 8.47 vs wasm3 1.01). A fork's README (andypeng2015/zwasm) says the 'majority match or beat wasmtime' on 29 benchmarks, which the canonical benchmarks doc does not support. Repo was previously clojurewasm/zwasm; github.com/clojurewasm/zwasm shows the same project.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime written from scratch benchmark faster than wasmtime wasm3 wasmer coremark interpreter JIT README' (zwasm result), then docs/benchmarks.md fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com/clojurewasm/zwasm

name: WAVM
baseline: Wasmer (LLVM backend), Wasmtime, V8 (Node.js), Lucet, Wasmer Singlepass
workload: libsodium 1.0.18 built-in cryptographic benchmark suite compiled to WASI, run on each WebAssembly runtime (macOS laptop, with a Linux x86_64 run for the LLVM-based runtimes).
claimed_speedup: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test'; 'WAVM was still about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); V8 (Node.js) second, then Wasmer Singlepass, Wasmtime, Lucet slowest. No per-test numbers in the README text (results are charts).
compiler_and_flags: All runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js from stock binaries); libsodium 1.0.18-stable built with system LLVM 11.1.0 via Homebrew, same default optimization flags for native and WebAssembly builds.
hardware: Intel CPU laptop (macOS) plus a Linux/x86_64 machine; CPU models not stated

caveats: Independent shootout, but data are from February 2021 and the repo's result charts are images; WAVM was not run on ARM. The newer 2022-12 results folder holds only images and raw data and the 2023/2026 posts on 00f.net are blocked; a search snippet for the 2026 post says wasmer is the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, so the ranking may have changed. WAVM's last commit is recent (2026-04-04) but its pace is slow.

name: aWsm
baseline: Wasmer; WAVM; Lucet; Node.js with Emscripten; wasm3 on microcontrollers
workload: PolyBench/C slowdown over native C, on x86-64, aarch64 (Raspberry Pi) and Cortex-M4/M7, for an ahead-of-time Wasm-to-LLVM compiler with a small C runtime.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 average slowdown over native: Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js + Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%. aarch64: aWsm 6.7%. Cortex-M7 40.2% and M4 24.9%, versus 'more than 10x' for the wasm3 interpreter on microcontrollers (links wasm3's Performance.md).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler through LLVM, so compile latency; the runtime is under 5K lines of C and the compiler under 3.5K lines of Rust; output is ELF objects; seven selectable memory-bounds-check mechanisms. Not a fit where interpreters or JIT are required.
caveats: README states 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README (EMSOFT 2020 paper and Sledge Middleware 2020 paper hold the details, but www2.seas.gwu.edu was blocked). Wasmtime is not in the x86-64 table (the table shows Wasmer, WAVM, Node.js+Emscripten, Lucet); Wasmer and Lucet versions are 2020-era. Rust compiler plus C runtime, so only the generated objects and runtime are callable from C++. Repo remains active (last commit 2026-07-13).
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly AOT OR JIT compiler paper artifact github evaluation wasmtime WAMR wasmer speedup single-pass baseline compiler' surfaced gwsystems/aWsm

name: LFI (Lightweight Fault Isolation)
baseline: LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers (not named in README; Wasmtime, Wasmer and wasm2c are the usual ones)
workload: Run-time overhead versus native code on the SPEC 2017 benchmark suite (compatible subset) for in-process software sandboxing of native Arm64 and x86-64 code, compared with the overhead WebAssembly sandboxing imposes.
claimed_speedup: LFI: 7% runtime overhead (Arm64) or 8% (x86-64) for full read and write isolation, 1.5% (Arm64) or 6% (x86-64) for writes only, versus 'LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly compilers, which incur upwards of 20% runtime overhead' (lfi-research branch README).
compiler_and_flags: LFI-patched LLVM toolchain (lfi-llvm-toolchain); flags not stated in README.
tradeoffs: Sandboxes native C/C++/assembly rather than Wasm bytecode: no stable binary format, no platform independence, Arm64 and x86-64 only (RISC-V experimental); needs an LFI compiler toolchain and a verifier; ~64K (Arm64) or ~3K (x86-64) sandboxes of up to 4 GiB per address space.
caveats: The Wasm comparison figure is a summary line in the README; the per-runtime numbers sit in the ASPLOS 2024 paper (Yedidia, Lightweight Fault Isolation), which was not opened (scs.stanford.edu and zyedidia.github.io blocked). The baseline is not named in the README, so the exact WebAssembly runtime is unconfirmed (confidence capped at 0.5). A search snippet quoting a different source gives Wasmtime about 150% and wasm2c about 197% of native run time; not verified here. Different execution model from a Wasm VM: it replaces Wasm rather than running it faster.

name: WAMR in Zig (cataggar/wamr)
baseline: wasmtime run (default Cranelift JIT)
workload: Cold start of a 36-byte no-op module (subprocess wall time, 20 samples after 3 warmups) comparing in-process JIT, AOT cold and warm modes against 'wasmtime run', plus CoreMark steady state.
claimed_speedup: Cold start median: in-process JIT (.fast preset) 1.430 ms vs wasmtime 6.964 ms (about 4.9x faster); AOT warm 1.182 ms; AOT cold 2.552 ms. CoreMark steady state: wasmtime 26,462.6 iter/s vs JIT .fast 12,002.8 and AOT 12,442.8, i.e. wasmtime about 2.1x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Zig build with -Djit=true -Doptimize=fast; scripts/bench_jit_coldstart.py; Zig version and wasmtime version not stated in the doc.
hardware: Azure VM, 8 vCPU, AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, x86_64
tradeoffs: Zig port of bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime kept as a separate fork (not drop-in for C++ callers without the Zig toolchain); passes the spec suite (257 .wast files, 65,135 assertions) per README; CLI is AOT/JIT only. Steady-state throughput is about half of wasmtime.
caveats: Cold-start win is on a trivial 36-byte module where wasmtime's fixed per-invocation cost dominates; the doc itself says wasmtime is about 2.1x faster on CoreMark. Single host, versions of wasmtime and Zig not stated, 5-star fork largely AI-assisted per its description. Process spawn time is included in the numbers.

name: wasmz
baseline: WAMR (iwasm 2.4.3); wasm3 v0.5.1; wasmi 2.0.0-beta.2
workload: Interpreter run time of fib(30) compiled from C, QuickJS fib(25) inside WASM (1.4 MB module) and esbuild bundling inside WASM (19 MB module), median of 20 runs after 5 warmups.
claimed_speedup: fib(30): wasmz 37.0 ms vs wasmi 38.4, wasm3 39.7, WAMR 49.6. QuickJS fib(25): 174.9 ms vs wasmi 184.4, wasm3 217.4, WAMR 242.9. esbuild: 909.5 ms vs wasmi 918.2, wasm3 2215.0 (WAMR excluded, it overflowed the stack). README: 'currently the fastest WebAssembly interpreter I have tested'.
compiler_and_flags: wasmz dev ReleaseFast (Zig); other runtimes' build flags not stated.
hardware: Linux 6.17.0-1010-azure x86_64 (Azure VM), CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Register-IR plus direct-threaded interpreter with accumulator registers and superinstructions; supports GC, SIMD, exceptions, threading, WASI preview 1; C and Zig APIs. Peak RSS on fib(30) 17.3 MB vs WAMR 11.0 MB.
caveats: First-party numbers, CPU not stated, and the wasm3 used is old v0.5.1 (current v0.9.0). The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (M4 Max, 2026-09-22) ranks wasmz behind wasm3 (geomean 1.59 vs 1.01), roughly level with WAMR (1.63) and ahead of wasmtime Pulley (2.09), and reports that wasmz fails six rows (2 wrong results, 2 traps, 2 crashes) and never collects GC structs. Treat the win over WAMR as unconfirmed.

name: wisp
baseline: wasmtime Winch (baseline compiler); wasmer Singlepass; wasmtime Cranelift on fib
workload: Whole-process wall time (including startup and compilation) of seven programs (primes, fib, matmul, raytrace, compress, json, regex) compiled to wasm32-wasip1, plus compile-only time for a 1.36 MB regex.wasm; median of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Compile-only regex.wasm: wisp 16 ms vs wasmtime Winch 24 ms, wasmer Singlepass 32 ms, wasmtime Cranelift 72 ms, wasmer Cranelift 82 ms. End to end: fib 34 wisp 0.022 s vs wasmtime Cranelift 0.024, Winch 0.031, wasmer Singlepass 0.028; raytrace 0.054 s vs Winch 0.066; json 0.263 s vs Winch 0.325; regex 0.308 s vs Winch 0.341 s.
compiler_and_flags: Release builds; wasmtime 49.0.1 and wasmer 7.5.0 release binaries; bench/run.py method documented in README.
tradeoffs: Compact (about 12,600 lines of Rust) runtime with validator, register-style interpreter and a single-pass AArch64 baseline compiler (macOS AArch64 only, Linux paths untested); passes 27,416 spec assertions on both engines; explicit bounds checks and no cross-block register allocation.
caveats: README states plainly that it is 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift end to end on six of seven programs, loses to Winch on primes, compress and matmul, and wasmtime/wasmer compile in parallel and write artefacts while wisp compiles single-threaded, so the compile-time comparison is not like for like. Own benchmarks only, 0 stars, 15 commits when viewed, very new. Rust and AArch64-only compiler, not callable from C++ without bindings.

name: Codon
baseline: PyPy 7.3.11 (pypy3) in the independent shootout; CPython 3.10.7 in the README claim
workload: Benchmarks-game programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, fasta, nbody, matmul, spectralnorm and others), single thread, Codon 0.15.5 versus PyPy3, best of up to 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: kostya/jit-benchmarks best times in s, Codon vs PyPy3: brainfuck 2.05 vs 8.77; brainfuck2 1.91 vs 11.03; binarytrees 1.0 vs 3.84; fasta 1.66 vs 3.19; knucleotide 2.69 vs 3.7; matmul 0.25 vs 0.36; nbody 2.23 vs 4.44; spectralnorm 0.53 vs 0.71. Slower on fannkuchredux 1.82 vs 0.71 and mandelbrot 0.65 vs 0.54. README: typical speedups over vanilla Python on the order of 10-100x or more.
compiler_and_flags: Docker images; Codon 0.15.5, PyPy 7.3.11 (python 3.9.16, gcc 10.2.1), CPython 3.10.7, C compiled with gcc 12.2.0; Codon flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80Gb DDR-4 3200 Mghz, docker on Ubuntu 22.10 (round 1, 2023-02-28)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler for a Python-like language (also a JIT decorator for use inside CPython) rather than a drop-in Python runtime: static typing, no GIL, a subset of Python and its libraries, compile step of 4-6 s in the shootout versus 0.2 s for PyPy startup. The compiler itself is C++/LLVM.
caveats: Independent shootout is a 2023 snapshot with Codon 0.15.5; Codon failed to run pidigits, regexdna and revcomp and lost to PyPy on fannkuchredux and mandelbrot. Best-time column excludes the 4-6 s compile time. Benchmarks are simple single-thread kernels. exaloop.io benchmarks page and the Codon paper (CC 2023) were not opened (blocked). README license shown as Apache-2.0 on the GitHub page; earlier Codon releases used BSL-1.1, so check the license of the version you use.

name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter (LuaJIT's interpreter, not its tracing JIT) and PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter
workload: Geometric mean over the repository's luabench Lua benchmark set, 5 repetitions each, interpreter vs LuaJIT's interpreter and vs PUC Lua 5.1.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (geometric average over all benchmarks, README).
compiler_and_flags: Release build through the repo's docker-based build (python3 ljr-build make release); compiler version and flags not stated in the README. run_bench.sh pins the process to one core with taskset.
tradeoffs: Interpreter and baseline JIT are generated automatically by the Deegen meta-compiler from bytecode semantic descriptions. x86-64 Linux only; GC is not implemented; Lua 5.1 only; package library (require/module) missing; tables use hidden classes instead of Lua's hash tables; optimizing JIT tier is future work.
caveats: Compares interpreters, not JITs: LuaJIT's optimizing tracing JIT is not beaten. The README states GC was turned off in the other Lua implementations for fairness. Numbers come from the author's own laptop. Snippet-only (paper not opened, arxiv/ACM blocked): a WebSearch snippet of the OOPSLA 2026 paper 'Deegen: A JIT-Capable VM Generator for Dynamic Languages' (doi 10.1145/3798246, arXiv 2411.11469) says that over 44 benchmarks the interpreter is 2.79x faster than PUC Lua and 1.31x faster than LuaJIT's interpreter, and the baseline JIT is 4.60x faster than PUC Lua but 33% slower than LuaJIT's optimizing JIT (faster on 13 of 44). Last commit Feb 2025, project work-in-progress.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Deegen LuaJIT Remake JIT-capable VM generator faster than LuaJIT paper github'; README opened on github.com

name: TPDE (TPDE-LLVM back-end)
baseline: LLVM -O0 code generation (clang/llc back-end)
workload: Compiling LLVM-IR to machine code at -O0 quality with TPDE-LLVM versus LLVM's -O0 back-end.
claimed_speedup: TPDE-LLVM compiles 10--20x faster than LLVM -O0 with similar code quality (README).
stars_or_usage: 671 stars; used for a Wasmtime back-end and in Umbra per search snippets
tradeoffs: Single-pass back-end aimed at -O0 quality baseline code, not optimized code. Targets ELF-based x86-64 and AArch64 (Armv8.1) only. Usable as library for JIT, as tpde-llc tool, or in Clang/Flang 22+ with a patch. Needs LLVM-IR (or another SSA IR through its adapters).
caveats: README gives only the headline ratio; evaluation setup is in the CGO 2026 paper (Schwarz, Kamm, Engelke; arXiv 2505.22610), which could not be opened (arxiv.org, home.cit.tum.de and docs.tpde.org blocked). Snippet-only from WebSearch results: 8-24x faster than LLVM -O0 on SPECint 2017 with geomean 12.15x on x86-64 and 18.96x on AArch64 and run-time within +-9%; Cranelift-IR back-end for Wasmtime compiles 4.27x faster than Cranelift's default register allocator but Cranelift's code runs 1.64x faster. SPEC CPU is proprietary so that evaluation is not fully reproducible. Compile-time win only; code quality is -O0 level, not comparable to V8 TurboFan or HotSpot C2.

name: CPython copy-and-patch JIT
baseline: CPython standard interpreter (tail-calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS), built with all optimizations
workload: pyperformance benchmark suite, JIT-enabled build versus the same CPython build without JIT.
claimed_speedup: Python 3.15 What's New: 7-8% geometric mean improvement for the JIT over the standard CPython interpreter on x86-64 Linux; 11-12% over the tail calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS; per-benchmark JIT vs no-JIT ranges from roughly 15% slowdown to over 100% speedup (ignoring the unpack_sequence microbenchmark).
compiler_and_flags: JIT stencils generated at build time with LLVM 21 (copy-and-patch, inspired by Xu and Kjolstad's paper); interpreter built with all optimizations; flags not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Experimental, off by default; enabled at build time with --enable-experimental-jit and at run time with PYTHON_JIT. Needs LLVM only at build time. Per the 3.14 notes it is not recommended for production and free-threaded builds do not support it. Machine-code unwinding support added in 3.15.
caveats: Compares the JIT to CPython's own interpreter, not to PyPy, so it does not beat the listed baselines; the claim is small (7-12% geomean) and some benchmarks slow down. Numbers are summarized from the linked doesjitgobrrr.com run (not opened, host not tried) and no CPU model is given. Included as a flagged entry for the copy-and-patch lineage.

name: Eclipse OpenJ9
baseline: OpenJDK 9 with HotSpot
workload: DayTrader3 application server benchmark: startup time, footprint and ramp-up of OpenJDK 9 with OpenJ9 versus OpenJDK 9 with HotSpot.
claimed_speedup: With AOT enabled, OpenJ9 startup time almost 40% lower than HotSpot; with AOT and -Xquickstart almost 50% lower; 40% less footprint during ramp up and about 60% less footprint after startup; similar peak throughput, OpenJ9 reached peak about 7 minutes faster (openj9-website benchmark page).
compiler_and_flags: JVM flags on the page: -Xshareclasses -Xscmx60M -Xscmaxaot8M (default AOT), -Xquickstart, and -Xscmx150M -Xscmaxaot120m -Xtune:virtualized (cloud tuning). Native build compiler not applicable.
hardware: One Intel Core i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz, 16GB RAM, 8 hardware threads (benchmark page)
license: EPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 (secondary GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0 for OpenJDK compatibility)
stars_or_usage: 3.5k stars; IBM Semeru runtime is built on it
tradeoffs: Complete JVM (JIT plus shared classes cache and AOT) that replaces HotSpot under OpenJDK. Wins are startup and memory, not peak throughput. Needs the shared class cache for the startup numbers. Separate code base, so behavior and flags differ from HotSpot.
caveats: First-party IBM/Eclipse benchmark on a 2017-era desktop CPU against OpenJDK 9; page copyright 2017-2024 so numbers may be old. The repository README itself has no numbers. Startup and footprint, not peak-throughput claims (peak is described as similar). The newer eclipse.dev benchmark pages (daytrader8, Java 17) were blocked and not opened; startup/footprint ranges in WebSearch snippets (10-30% faster startup, 31-38% smaller footprint) are snippet only.

name: GraalPy
baseline: CPython (README); PyPy is compared only in the independent shootout
workload: pyperformance suite run with 'pyperformance run' on CPython and on GraalPy, geomean over the pair-wise intersection of working benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: When JIT compiled, GraalPy runs Python code about 4x faster than CPython (geomean on the official Python Performance Benchmark Suite); without the Graal JIT, pure Python code runs about 4x slower than CPython (docs/user/Performance.md).
compiler_and_flags: Each interpreter installed through pyenv; JDK and GraalVM versions and flags not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Python 3.13 compatible runtime on the JVM/Truffle (embeddable in Java, native-image standalone). C extension performance varies; needs warmup, and JVM memory use is high (3 GB peaks in the shootout). Not usable directly from C++.
caveats: Java implementation, listed because the claim is against Python implementations and its JIT is the Graal compiler. First-party claim with no hardware. In the independent kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (GraalPy 22.3.1 vs PyPy3 7.3.11, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) GraalPy JVM mode beat PyPy on binarytrees (2.02 vs 3.84 s), fannkuchredux (0.36 vs 0.71 s), nbody (3.19 vs 4.44 s), spectralnorm (0.62 vs 0.71 s) but lost on brainfuck (14.22 vs 8.77 s), matmul (1.4 vs 0.36 s) and mandelbrot (0.84 vs 0.54 s).
found_via: WebSearch: 'Python JIT compiler "faster than PyPy" paper github C++ benchmark'; GraalPy README and Performance.md opened; shootout rows from kostya/jit-benchmarks README

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (also Luau and wasmtime named in README)
workload: Game-scripting style micro-benchmarks (call overhead, syscalls, integer math, array append, memcpy/memset, coroutines, fib(40), taylor series, sieve of 10M) comparing libriscv with binary translation (libtcc) against LuaJIT.
claimed_speedup: Gist for binary-translated libriscv vs LuaJIT: call overhead 2ns vs 156ns; syscall (0 args) 10ns vs 174ns; integer math 6ns vs 52ns; sieve(10M) 80ms vs 123ms; fib(40) median 66ns vs 66ns (equal). README: function call 3ns vs 50-150ns for other sandboxes, and libriscv can call a function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once.
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used in game-engine scripting per README
tradeoffs: It is a RISC-V emulator and sandbox: guest code must be compiled to RISC-V (gcc/clang cross compile), not Lua or JS source. Execution modes: interpreter, libtcc JIT binary translation (2-5x over interpreter per README), and full embedded binary translation (up to 20x per README). Very low call latency; memory and syscall access go through the sandbox.
caveats: Gist does not state CPU, compiler flags, LuaJIT version or date (last activity Oct 2025), so first-party tier C. The comparison is native-compiled guest code against Lua scripts, not the same program; benchmarks are hand-picked for game scripting; call overhead is subtracted from every result for both sides; on fib(40) the two are equal and the README itself lists interpreted libriscv vs LuaJIT as a separate gist. A JIT/binary translator claim, not a replacement for LuaJIT as a language implementation.
found_via: github.com/topics/jit?l=c%2B%2B listing (libriscv 'fastest RISC-V sandbox'); README and LuaJIT comparison gist opened

name: Pyston
baseline: CPython 3.8.12 (Pyston full) and CPython 3.7-3.10 (Pyston lite)
workload: Web serving macrobenchmarks (pyston/macrobenchmarks, a git submodule listed in the README build steps).
claimed_speedup: Pyston full is roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks; Pyston lite (JIT only extension module) is roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks (README).
tradeoffs: Pyston full is a fork of CPython 3.8.12 with a DynASM-based low-overhead JIT, quickening, attribute caching and build changes; API compatible but not ABI compatible, so C extensions must be rebuilt. Pyston lite is a pip-installable JIT extension (pyston_lite_autoload) for Python 3.7-3.10 that works with existing binary wheels.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no CPU, flags or run counts; compared with plain CPython 3.8 only, not PyPy. Repository description says no longer maintained and the last commit is Aug 2024, so the CPython base is out of date. Mixed licensing: repo LICENSE is Apache-2.0 but the CPython-derived code carries the PSF license.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Python JIT compiler "faster than PyPy" paper github C++ benchmark' (Pyston-lite / Pyston mentions); README opened on github.com

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler and runtime (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and V8 TurboFan; SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion
workload: Normalized compilation speed and execution speed of WebAssembly modules from the open-wasm-compiler-benchmark repo, WARP versus V8 and SpiderMonkey tiers and native clang code.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalized scores, compilation / execution): WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163; native clang 0.5 (comp. speed N/A) / 0.873.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide (scripts/benchmark/Readme.md, opened via raw.githubusercontent.com): clang/clang++, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, flags -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1; V8 built from source with gm.py x64.release; SpiderMonkey built with an optimized mozconfig. Versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler and runtime aimed at embedded systems (x86_64, aarch64, tricore; aarch32 not implemented), written in C++14 with no external dependencies in production code; 187 kB stripped binary (AArch64, Clang 17, macOS). Compiles ahead of time into an ELF-like artifact that the runtime instantiates.
caveats: Result is a normalized unitless chart in the README; how scores are normalized and the CPU model are not stated, so the tier is C although scripts are public. WARP execution speed (0.8172) is slightly below V8 TurboFan (0.8505) and native clang (0.873); the win is the combination of compile speed and execution speed. The original research paper (Scheidl, 'Valent-Blocks', iCCECE 2020, doi 10.1109/iCCECE49321.2020.9231154) was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'WebAssembly runtime JIT compiler faster than V8 Liftoff wasmtime paper open source github benchmark'; README and scripts/benchmark/Readme.md opened
